newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AGROKHLEB - Russian wheat harvest revised down.
newsitem.headline: AGROKHLEB - Russian wheat harvest revised down.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from the Agrokhleb Report, published by SovEcon Ltd, an independent research organisation specialising in agricultural production and trade in the former Soviet Union.
RUSSIA WHEAT HARVEST IN 1996 REVISED DOWN TO 34 MLN TONNES

MOSCOW, Oct 4 - SovEcon's forecast for Russia's total wheat production in 1996 has been revised down to 33-35 million tonnes from 36-39 million tonnes anticipated in late July. The revision is mainly due to losses in wheat plantings caused by the summer drought affecting the southern parts of the Volga river and the North Caucasus and adverse weather during harvesting in Siberia.

As a result of the summer drought, about nine and eight percent of wheat plantings in the North Caucasus and Povolzhsk respectively remained unharvested. The drought particularly affected Rostov Oblast, where the losses in wheat plantings accounted for around 20 pct of total area sown to wheat.

The delayed spring sowing campaign in West Siberia was exacerbated by rains in September. The harvest is lagging about two weeks behind normal progress. In Altai, the major wheat producing region in West Siberia, heavy rains have destroyed about one million hectares of crop plantings, mainly wheat. As a result, this wheat surplus region this year is likely to fail to meet its requirements in grain.
In East Siberia, wheat plantings were affected by the summer drought and current yields achieved from the harvested area are 16 percent down on last year (Table 1).

In quantitative terms, the anticipated wheat output might be enough to meet domestic requirements in milling wheat. However, a significant part of the wheat harvested this year is reported to be of low quality and could be used only for feed. Shares of milling wheats -- Class III and Class IV (which could be used in mixture with wheat of higher classes) -- are estimated at 32 percent and 24 percent of total output respectively.

In addition, state and farm grain stocks have been seriously depleted due to last year's crop failure. By August 1, wheat farm stocks had increased to 7 million tonnes, but were 18 percent down on last year.
Russia in 1996/97 seems likely to maintain its wheat and flour imports close to the 1995/96 level -- about four million tonnes, including flour in grain equivalent.
